questions.stem: A client who drinks heavily every day was admitted for surgery. When should the nurse expect withdrawal symptoms to begin?

options.text: About 6 to 24 hours after the last drink
Only if the client is given sedatives

rationale.correct: Alcohol withdrawal: early signs at 6 to 24 hours, seizures at 12 to 48 hours, delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours.

perOption.a: Early withdrawal (tremor, anxiety, tachycardia) begins within a day.
perOption.b: This is too late.
perOption.d: There is a delay of hours.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Predict the timing of alcohol withdrawal.

questions.stem: Three days after admission, a client with heavy alcohol use is confused, sweating and seeing bugs on the wall, with a heart rate of 128/min. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Benzodiazepines, seizure precautions and close monitoring for delirium tremens

rationale.correct: Delirium tremens: benzodiazepines, fluids, electrolytes, thiamine and a safe environment.

perOption.a: Delirium tremens is a medical emergency.
perOption.b: Antipsychotics alone can lower the seizure threshold.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the CIWA-Ar scale for a client in alcohol withdrawal?

options.text: To measure withdrawal severity and guide symptom-triggered medication

rationale.correct: Use CIWA-Ar for symptom-triggered treatment of alcohol withdrawal.

perOption.a: Scores guide benzodiazepine dosing.
perOption.b: It measures withdrawal, not the disorder.

questions.stem: A malnourished client with alcohol use disorder is confused and has an unsteady gait. Which prescription should the nurse give before IV dextrose?

rationale.correct: Give thiamine before glucose in at-risk clients to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

perOption.a: Giving glucose before thiamine can bring on or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.
perOption.b: This is helpful but not the priority before glucose.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client taking disulfiram asks what to avoid. Which statement shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll avoid alcohol in any form, including some mouthwashes, cough syrups and sauces."
"I can have one drink a day."
"I can stop disulfiram and drink the same day."

rationale.correct: Disulfiram: avoid all hidden alcohol sources; the reaction includes flushing, vomiting and hypotension.

perOption.a: Even small amounts of alcohol cause a severe reaction.
perOption.b: Any alcohol causes a reaction.
perOption.c: The effect lasts up to 2 weeks.
perOption.d: It deters drinking; it doesn't reduce cravings.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: Which findings suggest opioid withdrawal?

options.text: Yawning, runny nose, dilated pupils, diarrhea and muscle aches

rationale.correct: Opioid withdrawal: flu-like symptoms, mydriasis, piloerection, GI upset and cravings.

perOption.a: These are typical; they're very uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening.
perOption.b: These suggest overdose.
perOption.c: These are more typical of alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client with opioid use disorder is starting buprenorphine. When should the first dose be given?

options.text: When the client is already in mild to moderate withdrawal
Right after the client last used heroin
At the same time as a full opioid agonist
Only after 30 days without any opioids

rationale.correct: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist; start it when withdrawal is already present.

perOption.a: Giving it too early can trigger sudden (precipitated) withdrawal.
perOption.b: This risks precipitated withdrawal.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: What must be confirmed before a client starts naltrexone for opioid use disorder?

options.text: The client has been opioid-free for about 7 to 10 days
The client is currently using opioids
The client has a normal blood glucose
The client has been drinking alcohol

rationale.correct: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist; the client must be opioid-free first.

perOption.a: Naltrexone blocks opioids and causes severe withdrawal if opioids are still present.
perOption.b: This would cause withdrawal.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client is unresponsive, with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6/min. What does the nurse suspect, and what should be given?

rationale.correct: Opioid overdose: support breathing and give naloxone; watch for re-sedation.

perOption.a: This triad is typical of opioid overdose.
perOption.b: Stimulants cause dilated pupils and agitation.
perOption.c: Withdrawal causes agitation, not coma with pinpoint pupils.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client who used cocaine has chest pain, a heart rate of 132/min and a blood pressure of 188/108 mm Hg. What is the main concern?

rationale.correct: Stimulant toxicity: tachycardia, hypertension, chest pain, hyperthermia and agitation.

perOption.a: Cocaine causes coronary vasospasm, ischemia and dysrhythmias.
perOption.b: This is more typical of opioids.
perOption.d: This isn't the main concern now.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client says, "I don't have a drinking problem. I can stop anytime I want." Which defense mechanism is this?

rationale.correct: Denial is a major barrier to treatment in substance use disorders.

perOption.a: Refusing to acknowledge the problem is common in substance use.
perOption.b: This channels impulses into acceptable activities.
perOption.c: This attributes one's feelings to others.
perOption.d: This is returning to earlier behavior.

rationale.correct: Families benefit from support groups such as Al-Anon to stop enabling.

perOption.a: Protecting the client from consequences allows the drinking to continue.
perOption.b: This protects the drinking.

questions.stem: Which question is part of the CAGE screening tool for alcohol use?

options.text: "Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking?"
"How old were you when you first drank?"

rationale.correct: CAGE: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; two or more yes answers suggest a problem.

perOption.a: C = Cut down.
perOption.b: This isn't a screening item.

questions.stem: For each feature, indicate whether it is more typical of delirium or dementia.

rows.text: Sudden onset over hours to days
Level of awareness that fluctuates during the day
Usually reversible when the cause is treated

rationale.correct: Delirium: acute, fluctuating, inattentive, often reversible. Dementia: gradual and progressive.

perOption.r2:c1: Fluctuating awareness is typical of delirium.
perOption.r2:c2: Consciousness is usually stable in dementia until late.
perOption.r4:c1: Delirium often resolves when the cause is treated.
perOption.r5:c1: Inattention is a core feature of delirium.
perOption.r5:c2: Attention is often preserved early in dementia.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with Alzheimer's disease keeps asking for her mother, who died years ago. What is the best response?

options.text: "You're thinking about your mother. Tell me about her."

rationale.correct: Use validation and redirection in advanced dementia; avoid arguing.

perOption.a: Validation addresses the feelings without arguing.
perOption.b: Repeated reorientation to a painful fact can cause distress.

questions.stem: A client with dementia becomes more confused and agitated in the late afternoon. Which intervention helps?

options.text: Keep a consistent routine and good lighting, and reduce stimulation in the evening
Schedule baths and visitors in the late afternoon

rationale.correct: Sundowning: routine, daytime activity, lighting and a calm evening environment.

perOption.a: Structure and lighting reduce sundowning.
perOption.b: This adds stimulation at a bad time.
